# PRD 001: Concept Graph

**Schema**: pij/prd · **Source**: 001-concept-graph.dd.json · **Sections**: 8

## Meta

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| title | PRD 001: Concept Graph |
| status | draft |
| updated | 2026-11-11 |
| owner | project lead |
| summary | Concept Graph lets agents turn the operator's work (calls, documents, workshops, projects) into addressable, embedded knowledge graphs that they can search, walk and join. It is a Rust CLI and local daemon over plain files in git, built small first and changed cheaply as agents use it. |

<a id="why"></a>

## Why

The operator's work is spread across calls, transcripts, documents, workshops and repos. Notes and summaries lose the shape of it: what is contested, what blocks what, which constraint (a piece of legislation, say) frames a whole problem space, and where each claim came from. A live concept graph built by agents during a design workshop showed the value: a high-fidelity map of a problem that other agents could reason over and that became the raw material for requirements and prototypes. That graph was one JSON file and one HTML page. Doing this across every customer, project and call needs a real tool: permanent addresses so documents can link to nodes, many graphs that link and join across each other, embeddings on every field so like content is found anywhere, and a fast CLI that agents in Claude Code or Copilot use as their main way in.

<a id="actors"></a>

## Actors

| id | name | need |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a-operator | the operator | Project all their work into graphs they and their agents can question, walk and build from. |
| a-agent | external agent | Build and use graphs through a CLI it can learn from built-in docs, with errors that say what to do next. |
| a-teammate | teammate | Keep their own graphs in a shared repo, link to others' graphs, and merge without pain. |

<a id="goals"></a>

## Goals

| id | goal |
| --- | --- |
| g-1 | An agent can seed a graph, ingest a transcript into it with evidence pointing at exact lines, and answer questions over it, using only the CLI and its docs. |
| g-2 | Any node can be linked from any document by a permanent address, and found again. |
| g-3 | Several graphs can be loaded together and walked, searched and joined as if they were one, without changing any of them. |
| g-4 | Like content is found across nodes, fields and graphs by similarity. |
| g-5 | A basic version works early and every change is cheap, so agents use it themselves from the start. |

<a id="non-goals"></a>

## Non goals

| id | text |
| --- | --- |
| n-1 | Serving a team over the network. The v1 daemon is local only, one per machine. |
| n-2 | A shared or remote UI. The v1 UI (req-104 to req-115) is a local, single-user view on this machine; editing in the UI, a Cypher console, multi-user use and saved layouts come later (decided 2026-11-11). |
| n-3 | Massive graphs. Tens of thousands of nodes per graph is the design scale; millions are not. |
| n-4 | Fixed speed targets. Benchmarks report what we see and what each feature costs. |
| n-5 | Policing agents. The ontology guides with warnings; it never refuses. |
| n-6 | Writing through Cypher. Cypher is read-only; writes go through CLI verbs. |
| n-7 | Auto-starting the daemon, or a CLI mode that reads files without it. |
| n-8 | LadybugDB in v1. The graph lives in our own in-memory Rust code (umx-graph, core code, not a port, per q-12); a database adapter and a graph-store port can come later if a second store earns it. |
| n-9 | Capturing audio or captions. Transcripts come from existing capture tools. |
| n-10 | Splitting or merging graphs, and moving nodes between graphs, in v1. Rename and re-file are enough. |
| n-11 | A special hub-graph feature. A hub is an ordinary graph whose nodes link into other graphs (req-21). |
| n-12 | Overlays as a separate kind of thing (retired 2026-11-10). Joining graphs is loading them into one space and linking across them. |
| n-13 | Windows, for now (decided 2026-11-10). umx targets macOS and Linux. If it comes later, the CLI-to-daemon transport becomes a named pipe and the service uses Task Scheduler; both sit behind adapters. |
| n-14 | Display hints in the vocabulary (D42, 2026-11-10). Types, statuses and relations carry no colour, shape or border. How a graph looks belongs to the UI that renders it, not to the graph files. |

| req-148 | --raised-in on node add and batch | `umx node add --raised-in &lt;anchor&gt;` adds the node and a raised_in edge from it to the anchor in one write; a refusal of either writes nothing. `umx batch --raised-in &lt;anchor&gt;` gives every node the batch adds (not edits, notes, status moves or edge lines) a raised_in edge to the anchor; a node add line's own `raised_in` names its anchor instead. The anchor is a node of the graph or an address in another (`umx:&lt;graph&gt;/&lt;id&gt;`), resolved exactly as `umx edge add` resolves an end, so it is refused or warned about as edge add would be; a batch's anchor is resolved once, before any line runs, and one that does not resolve refuses the whole batch with edge add's own error. An anchor of a type raised_in does not expect (segment, meeting, event, transcript, phase) warns relation_endpoint_unexpected and is stored; a far anchor's type is read only from an open graph. Node add's reply names the edge (`raised_in_edge`); each batch row names its edge (`raised_in_edge`, null in a dry run) and anchor (`raised_in`). | a-agent | should | [x] shipped | umx tests a_node_raised_in_an_anchor_gets_its_edge_in_the_same_write, an_unresolvable_anchor_is_refused_as_edge_add_refuses_it and a_batch_raised_in_an_anchor_links_every_node_it_adds pass; node.md, batch.md, ingest.md, time.md, usage 179 and the ingest route teach it. | D71; the internal time review 4.B B2 (a default anchor for a batch) and step 8; ws008 TM4, plan 177; project manager 2026-11-13 | — | — | — |
| req-149 | Declared spines | `umx graph spine confirm &lt;graph&gt; &lt;candidate&gt;` stores a proposed anchor-type candidate's declaration in graph.json's `spines` unchanged (a built-in candidate is refused, spine_builtin_candidate, with set as its next); `umx graph spine set &lt;graph&gt; --file &lt;decl.json&gt;` stores one the builder writes, replacing the declared spine of the same name; `umx graph spine show &lt;graph&gt; [&lt;name&gt;]` places the graph on each declared spine now and reports cover and spread as propose does; `umx graph spine remove &lt;graph&gt; &lt;name&gt;` drops one. Every name in a declaration is the graph's vocabulary or std (spine_name_unknown names the part), a graph has at most one main spine (spine_main_taken), and a refusal writes nothing. Writes go through the checked graph.json write. The first declared spine raises graph.json to format 6 (FORMAT_SPINES), which an older umx refuses (graph_format_newer); a graph with none keeps its format. Placement gains by_rule, fixed in the service with named settings (no expressions): a node nothing else places sits in the middle band of its neighbours placed by data, one link away; a rule placement never feeds another and the anchors' parent is never placed by rule (D71; time review 5.3 and step 9). | a-agent | should | [x] shipped | umx tests a_declared_spine_round_trips_through_set_show_and_remove, confirm_stores_the_proposed_declaration_unchanged and a_spine_declaration_is_checked_before_it_is_stored, umx-core the_spines_format_is_written_for_a_spine_and_refused_by_an_older_reader and umx-services a_node_linked_to_placed_nodes_sits_in_their_middle_band_by_rule pass; graph.md, time.md, usage 187 and the build route teach it. | D71; the internal time review 5.2, 5.3 and step 9; architect's FORMAT_SPINES ruling (2026-11-12); ws008 TM5, plan 194; the project manager 2026-11-13 | — | — | — |

The anchor resolves exactly as `--raised-in`'s does (edge add's end: its refusals byte for byte, its warnings, relation_endpoint_unexpected against raised_in's target types, a secured far anchor's type never read); a refusal makes no move. <a id="open-questions"></a>

## Open questions

| id | question | default | answer | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| q-01 | What is the CLI called? | `umx`. | `umx` (decided 2026-11-09). Checked clear of macOS, Homebrew, Debian/Ubuntu, Arch/AUR, Fedora, winget, Scoop, Chocolatey, crates.io and PyPI; npm's `umx` installs no command. | answered |
| q-02 | Where do secured graphs live, given anyone who can read the repo can read them? | In their own private repo or an untracked folder; the CLI warns when a secured graph sits in a repo with a remote. | — | open |
| q-03 | Which embedding models by default? | Hosted `text-embedding-3-small` at 256 dimensions for open graphs. Secured graphs use word search only until a local model is added; that model is picked by a short bake-off among models trained to be cut short (nomic-embed-text-v1.5, EmbeddingGemma-300M, arctic-embed-l-v2, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B), or runs at its native size. | — | open |
| q-04 | Are customer graphs secured by default? | Yes when they hold client transcripts or documents; open for the operator's own concept and project graphs. | — | open |
| q-05 | Can secured graphs be compared with open graphs by similarity? | No in v1: graphs on different models cannot be compared. Later, an open graph can compute a local vector set on demand to compare with a secured graph. | — | open |
| q-06 | What form do node ids take? | ULID; fully random ids for secured graphs so creation time does not leak. | — | open |
| q-07 | What is the starter ontology for `umx graph new`? | The vocabulary proven in the live concept graph work: problem, actor, option, mechanism, criterion, question, decision, tension, precedent, capability; statuses agreed, contested, open, ruled-out, proposed, context; relations supports, undercuts, depends-on, blocks, conflicts-with, answers, part-of, alternative-to, raises, owned-by. Add relations tests, possibly-same-as and criterion-for, and statuses leaning and acknowledged, which the field session needed. | — | open |
| q-08 | How does the daemon find graphs? | See req-56: `umx graph add &lt;path&gt; --alias &lt;name&gt;` registers a graph in a per-machine registry. | — | open |
| q-09 | How do we query edge fields with Cypher, which cypher-parser may not support? | Extend or vendor cypher-parser (MIT) when the first query needs it. | — | open |
| q-10 | What data do we test and benchmark on? | A realistic synthetic set (transcripts, documents, a workshop) generated by agents, with no client data. | — | open |
| q-11 | How is Word document evidence opened? | Open the document and highlight the quoted text; there is no reliable paragraph link. | — | open |
| q-12 | Is the in-memory graph our core code, or the first adapter behind a graph-store port (so LadybugDB could be a second adapter)? | Answered in blueprint 001 d-1: the in-memory graph is our own core code (umx-graph), not a port. A GraphStore trait is extracted only if a second store earns it. | — | answered |
